title: Ambient temperature and mortality from unintentional cocaine overdose

claims.statement: In New York City in 1993 to 1995, days on which that day's or the previous day's highest temperature reached 31.1 °C (88 °F) (146 of 1,095 days, here called hot days), compared with other days, were associated with more deaths certified by the city's medical examiner as unintentional cocaine overdose: 2.34 a day against 1.76 (341 deaths on hot days, 1,667 on other days), a third more (Marzuk et al., 1998); by the editors' calculation a rate ratio of 1.33 (95% CI 1.18 to 1.49), or about 85 deaths more than the other-day rate predicts, some 4 in 100 of the 2,008 cocaine overdose deaths of those three years. The days were compared without any adjustment for season, day of the week, holidays or trend, and nobody's heat exposure, amount used or pattern of use was known. Deaths from opiates without cocaine were 0.81 against 0.71 a day and other overdose deaths 0.08 on both kinds of day, neither difference significant, but by the editors' calculation the opiate rate ratio (1.14, 0.93 to 1.38) did not differ significantly from the cocaine one (ratio of the two 1.17, 0.93 to 1.47), so the paper's reading that the rise was specific to cocaine is not established; the share of homicide and traffic victims with cocaine in their blood was much the same on hot and other days (18.9 against 19.5 in 100; 9.5 against 10.3 in 100), which the authors read as cocaine use not rising on hot days; and opiates were also found in about 6 in 10 of the deaths counted as cocaine overdoses. The temperature threshold was chosen from the 1990 to 1992 overdose deaths and the dates of heat deaths with cocaine, then tested on the 1993 to 1995 deaths; of 40 tested deaths certified as due to overheating (hyperthermia) in 1990 to 1995, 10 had a breakdown product of cocaine in the body. In a laboratory experiment (Crandall et al., 2002), 7 healthy adults aged 23 to 37 who had never used cocaine were heated at rest in a suit carrying water at 46 °C after one intranasal dose of cocaine (2 mg per kg, described by the authors as low; study conditions) and, on another day in random order, after the same dose of lidocaine, a local anaesthetic used as the comparison (called placebo in the abstract): before heating, core temperature did not differ (36.79 against 36.75 °C), but during heating it rose more after cocaine (P < 0.001; to about 37.8 against 37.5 °C after about 38 minutes, read from the paper's figure and approximate); the skin's blood vessels began to widen, and sweating began, at a core temperature about 0.3 °C higher (37.37 against 37.06 °C and 37.38 against 37.07 °C; by the editors' calculation, 95% CIs of about 0.11 to 0.51 and 0.16 to 0.46 °C); at a core temperature of 37.86 °C, skin blood flow was 49 against 70 in 100 of its maximum and sweat rate 0.8 against 1.0 mg per cm² per minute (how many people reached that temperature is not stated); and people felt less hot at the same core temperature. Heat production was not measured, so the authors' conclusion that cocaine raises body temperature mainly by impairing heat loss is an inference; they expect larger doses to add heat production, say the results may not apply to people who use cocaine regularly, and did not test their suggestion that hot weather and crowded clubs amplify the effect. Neither study followed people who used cocaine in hot weather. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Marzuk et al. (1998), New York City 1993–1995: cocaine overdose deaths 2.34 a day (SD 1.68; 341 deaths on 146 hot days) against 1.76 (SD 1.37; 1,667 on 949 other days), Mann-Whitney z = 3.98, P < .001, 33% higher mean; opiate overdose deaths without cocaine 0.81 (SD 0.94) against 0.71 (SD 0.86), P = .28; other overdose deaths 0.08 against 0.08, P = .69; cocaine in blood of homicide victims 18.9% (136/719) against 19.5% (766/3,919), of traffic victims aged 15–54 9.5% (12/126) against 10.3% (71/689); opiates in 57.1% and 61.7% of cocaine overdose deaths (hot, other days); deaths certified as hyperthermia 1990–1995: benzoylecgonine in 10 of 40 tested (21% of all 48). Editors' calculations (Poisson, ignoring overdispersion and the reported autocorrelation of 0.12, so somewhat too narrow): cocaine rate ratio 1.33 (1.18 to 1.49); opiates 1.14 (0.93 to 1.38); ratio of the two 1.17 (0.93 to 1.47); about 85 excess deaths, about 4% of 2,008. Crandall et al. (2002), 7 cocaine-naive adults, cocaine against lidocaine, mean ± SE: core temperature before heating 36.79 ± 0.01 against 36.75 ± 0.08 °C; greater rise during heating, P < 0.001 (about 37.8 against 37.5 °C after about 38 min, read from Figure 1, approximate); onset of skin vasodilation at 37.37 ± 0.09 against 37.06 ± 0.07 °C (P = 0.01) and of sweating at 37.38 ± 0.09 against 37.07 ± 0.06 °C (P = 0.002), slopes unchanged; at 37.86 °C, skin vascular conductance 49 ± 9 against 70 ± 5% of maximum (P = 0.03) and sweat rate 0.8 ± 0.2 against 1.0 ± 0.1 mg/cm² per minute (P = 0.04), number contributing not stated; before heating, mean arterial pressure 93 ± 3 against 85 ± 3 mm Hg and heart rate 74 ± 5 against 67 ± 4 beats/min. Editors' calculation from the rounded P values: threshold shifts of 0.31 °C (95% CI about 0.11 to 0.51 and 0.16 to 0.46 °C).
